Illegitimacy in literature refers to the condition of being born outside wedlock, a social category that carries profound implications for inheritance, legitimacy, and personal identity. In early modern and Victorian literature especially, illegitimacy becomes a narrative driver—a fact that generates plot complications, moral dilemmas, and opportunities for exploring questions of justice, identity, and social hierarchy. The illegitimate child often becomes a figure of symbolic transgression or sympathetic outsider, revealing the arbitrary nature of social categories.

In pre-modern and early modern societies, illegitimate birth automatically excluded a person from inheritance and certain social positions, creating material and psychological stakes. The stigma was both legal and social. The illegitimate child often harbors resentment toward the father who denied recognition or toward the legitimate heirs who benefit from legal privilege. This resentment becomes a psychological motor for narrative action. Literature uses illegitimacy to explore the tension between biological kinship and legal legitimacy. What is really yours when law denies your paternity? The category exposes the arbitrariness of social order.

In King Lear, Edmund's illegitimacy drives his villainy. He seeks to undo the legitimate claims of his half-brother Edgar and displace the rightful heir through deception and manipulation. Illegitimacy can evoke sympathy or complicity depending on how the narrative treats the character's response—whether they accept or resist their exclusion. Literature reveals how social structures create criminals and how legal status generates moral and political chaos.

The category is gendered. Illegitimate daughters face particular sexual and economic vulnerability, while illegitimate sons often pursue status through cunning or force. Patriarchal inheritance makes illegitimacy differently consequential for men and women. Edmund is the classic literary bastard whose resentment and ambition drive Shakespearean tragedy. Edgar is his legitimate half-brother, whose legitimacy becomes ironically uncertain when Edmund's plots make him appear the traitor. King Lear is the play that makes illegitimacy a central plot engine, exploring how legal status generates moral and political chaos. Inheritance is the legal and economic system that makes illegitimacy a consequential category. Social class is marked permanently by illegitimacy with exclusion from certain social positions and privileges. Betrayal and vengeance are the strategies illegitimate characters often pursue as means of overcoming their exclusion.
